description: Hard water, pH, dissolving, hydrogen bond

questions.stem: 'Hard water' owes its hardness primarily to the dissolved salts of:
questions.explanation: Hardness of water is caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium ions, usually as bicarbonates (temporary hardness — removed by boiling) or chlorides and sulphates (permanent hardness — removed by ion-exchange resin or washing soda). Hard water lathers poorly with soap (forms scum) and leaves scale deposits in boilers and pipes. Soft water has sodium / potassium salts instead.

questions.explanation: Pure (distilled) water is a very poor conductor because it has very few ions (it self-ionises only slightly: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻). Tap water, sea water and sweaty skin are good conductors because of dissolved salts that release ions. 'Not at all' is too strong — pure water has some conductivity but extremely low. Even so, never use water on an electric fire — the impurities in real water conduct.

questions.stem: Temporary hardness of water can be removed by:
questions.explanation: Temporary hardness is due to calcium and magnesium BI-carbonates that on boiling break down into insoluble carbonates that settle out — Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ ↓ + H₂O + CO₂. This is why an old kettle has scale deposits. Permanent hardness (due to chlorides/sulphates) cannot be removed by boiling; you need washing soda, zeolite, or ion-exchange resins.

questions.stem: A water molecule is bent (not linear) because of:

options.option_text: The two lone pairs on oxygen

questions.explanation: The oxygen atom in H₂O has two bond pairs (O-H) and two lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs, pushing the O-H bonds together. The resulting H-O-H angle is ~104.5° instead of the straight 180°. This bent shape gives water its polarity, and the polarity gives rise to hydrogen bonding — which explains water's many anomalous properties (high boiling point, ice floats, high specific heat).

questions.stem: Heavy water, used in some nuclear reactors, is chemically:

options.option_text: D₂O, water with deuterium instead of ordinary hydrogen
Sea water with high salt content

questions.explanation: Heavy water — D₂O — has deuterium (²H), hydrogen's heavier stable isotope, in place of normal ¹H. It is used in pressurised heavy-water reactors (like India's CANDU-type PHWRs at Rawatbhata, Kakrapar) as a neutron moderator — it slows neutrons without absorbing them, so the reactor can use natural (unenriched) uranium. Density ~11 % higher than ordinary water; tastes indistinguishable but toxic in large amounts.

questions.stem: Water is called a 'universal solvent' because:

options.option_text: Its polarity lets it dissolve many substances
It has a high boiling point

questions.explanation: Water is a strongly polar molecule — the O end carries partial negative charge, the H ends partial positive. Ionic compounds (NaCl) and polar molecules (sugar) get surrounded by water molecules, are pulled apart, and dissolve. Non-polar substances (oils, petrol) do not. So the 'universal' label is a bit of an exaggeration — it is a universal solvent only for polar and ionic compounds.

questions.stem: The pH value of normal rainwater (saturated with atmospheric CO₂) is approximately:
questions.explanation: Normal rainwater has pH ~5.6 — slightly acidic because atmospheric CO₂ dissolves in it to form carbonic acid. Rain below pH 5.0 is called 'acid rain' — driven by SO₂ (from burning coal, smelters) and NOₓ (from vehicles and power plants) forming sulphuric and nitric acids. Acid rain damages forests, fish populations and heritage monuments (the Taj Mahal being a famous example).
